guides.title: Knot Anatomy: Bight, Loop, Standing End
guides.summary: The vocabulary and mechanics of rope: standing end, working end, bight, loop, turn and nip, how friction and curvature make a knot hold, how much strength a knot costs, and how to read, tie, dress and inspect knots by understanding their structure rather than memorising sequences.

sections.heading: Why the Vocabulary Comes First
sections.body:
Most people learn knots the way they learn a card trick: by copying a sequence of hand movements until the shape appears. This works for one or two knots and then stops working. The moment the rope is a different diameter, or the far end is unavailable, or the knot must be tied around a rail rather than through a ring, or the light is bad and the rope is wet, the memorised sequence collapses. What survives those conditions is understanding the parts, because a knot is not a sequence of movements. It is a geometry, and a geometry can be reconstructed from any starting position by someone who knows what shape they are trying to produce.

The vocabulary that describes those parts is small — perhaps a dozen terms carry almost all of the useful meaning — and it is remarkably stable across sailing, climbing, caving, rescue, arboriculture, fishing, rigging and scouting. The core of it was systematised in English by Clifford Ashley in The Ashley Book of Knots, published in 1944, which catalogued around 3,900 knots and gave each an index number still cited today as an ABOK number. Ashley's terminology was not invented by him; he collected it from working sailors and riggers, which is why it sounds practical rather than academic. A bight, a turn, a nip: these are words that were used by people who needed to shout instructions across a deck.

The immediate payoff of learning them is that knot instructions become readable. "Form a bight in the standing part, pass the working end through, and dress the knot before loading" is a complete and unambiguous specification of an action, comprehensible without a diagram, and it can be given over a radio to someone you cannot see. Compare it with the pictorial alternative, which requires that the reader be holding the rope in the same orientation as the illustrator.

The deeper payoff is diagnostic. Knowing the parts lets you look at a finished knot and say whether it is correct — whether the working end emerges where it should, whether the parts are parallel rather than crossed, whether the load will fall on the strand that is meant to take it. This is the difference between someone who can tie a bowline and someone who can check a bowline, and in any activity where a knot holds weight, the second skill is worth far more than the first. A great many rope accidents involve knots that were tied nearly right by people who had never been taught what right looks like.

There is one further reason to start here. Almost every knot in common use is assembled from the same handful of elements in different arrangements. Once those elements are familiar, the apparent forest of hundreds of named knots resolves into a much smaller number of structural ideas, and learning a new knot becomes a matter of recognising a familiar pattern rather than memorising another trick.

sections.heading: The Ends and Parts of a Working Rope
sections.body:
A rope in use has named regions, and the names are relative to what you are doing rather than fixed properties of the rope. The same physical end can be the working end in one operation and the standing end in the next.

The working end, also called the running end or the bitter end in some traditions, is the end you are actively manipulating. It is the part that gets threaded, passed and tucked. In instructions it is the subject of most verbs.

The standing end is the other end: the one that is not being handled, typically because it is attached to something, held by someone, or simply lying there. In a rope tied to a boat, the standing end is at the boat.

The standing part is the more useful term, and the one beginners most often miss. It is not an end at all; it is the length of rope between the knot and the standing end — the section that will actually carry the load. Almost every knot instruction refers to it, because most knots are built by wrapping or tucking the working end around or through the standing part. When someone says a knot "jams the working end against the standing part", they are describing the mechanism by which it holds.

The tail is what remains of the working end after the knot is complete: the short piece sticking out. Its length matters more than beginners expect. Too short and the knot can work loose or invert under cyclic loading; too long and it is a snagging hazard and a temptation to clip into the wrong strand. Conventions vary by discipline, but a widely taught rule of thumb for life-safety knots is a tail of at least ten times the rope diameter, so roughly 10 to 12 centimetres on an 11 millimetre climbing rope. Sailing practice is generally more relaxed, fishing practice tighter.

Two further terms describe rope condition rather than geometry. Lay is the direction of twist in a traditional twisted rope, described as right-hand or left-hand, and it matters because some knots behave differently with or against the lay. Slack is unloaded rope, and the phrase "take up the slack" is the ordinary instruction to remove it before loading.

Finally, a rope is technically not a rope once it has a purpose. Sailors call a rope that has been assigned a job a line, and give it a specific name — sheet, halyard, painter, warp — reserving "rope" for the raw stock on the reel. This is not affectation; on a vessel where a dozen lines are within reach, "ease the jib sheet" is instantly actionable and "let out that rope" is not. The general lesson holds everywhere rope is used seriously: precise names are a safety feature.

sections.heading: The Bight: The Universal Building Block
sections.body:
A bight is a bend or curve in the rope in which the two adjacent parts do not cross one another. Take any section of line, double it back on itself into a U shape, and you have formed a bight. Crucially, the rope has not been crossed over itself; the two legs lie parallel. If you were to pull the ends apart, the bight would simply straighten out and disappear, leaving no trace.

The strict definition matters because the distinction between a bight and a loop is the single most common vocabulary error in knotting, and it changes the meaning of instructions. A bight is an open curve. A loop, in the precise sense, involves a crossing. Ashley and most modern technical sources maintain this distinction rigorously; casual usage often does not, which is why a beginner reading a badly written instruction can produce quite the wrong shape while following it faithfully.

The bight is the universal building block for three reasons. First, an enormous number of knots are constructed by passing a bight somewhere rather than by passing an end, and passing a bight is faster because you are moving the middle of the rope rather than threading a long tail through a small aperture. Second, doubling the rope through a bight is how a knot is made to hold a load in two strands rather than one, which is the structural basis of most loop knots. Third — and this is the reason it matters most in the field — a knot that can be tied in a bight can be tied anywhere along a rope without access to either end.

That last property has a specific name: tying "on a bight" or "in the bight" means forming the knot in the middle of the line, with both ends still attached to whatever they are attached to. The figure-eight on a bight, the alpine butterfly and the bowline on a bight are all examples. In practice this is enormously valuable. If a rope is already anchored at both ends, or one end is fifty metres below you, or the end is buried under a load, a knot that requires the end is simply unavailable, and knowing which knots can be tied in the bight is a genuine operational skill rather than a piece of trivia.

The phrase also survives in a well-known safety warning: never stand in the bight of a line. On deck, on a tow, or anywhere a rope under tension curves around something, the area inside that curve is where the rope will sweep if it comes free or the load shifts. Ropes under tension store elastic energy and release it violently — a parted mooring line can travel faster than a person can react and has caused fatal injuries. The anatomical term and the safety rule are the same word for the same reason: the inside of a curve in loaded rope is a place with a name because it is a place that kills people.

sections.heading: Loops, Crossing Turns, and Which Part Lies on Top
sections.body:
A loop is formed when the rope crosses over itself, so that the two parts of the line touch and one lies above the other. That single crossing point is what separates a loop from a bight, and it is also the seed of almost every knot, because a crossing is the first place where friction can be developed between one part of the rope and another.

Loops come in two handednesses, and the distinction is not decorative. In an overhand loop, the working end passes over the standing part at the crossing. In an underhand loop, the working end passes under. The finished shapes look confusingly similar at a glance, and choosing the wrong one is the most frequent cause of a knot coming out as something else entirely. The classic demonstration is the bowline: made with the correct crossing you get a bowline, made with the crossing reversed you get a slip knot or a left-hand bowline, which is a measurably weaker and less stable knot. Similarly, a sheet bend tied with the working end emerging on the wrong side becomes the notoriously unreliable left-hand sheet bend.

A third term, the crossing turn, describes a loop made by passing the rope around an object — or around its own standing part — so that the crossing lies flat and the two parts are visible where they cross. Many knot books use "crossing turn" precisely because "loop" is overloaded: in ordinary speech, "loop" also means the finished eye of a loop knot, such as the fixed eye of a bowline that you clip a carabiner into. Technical writing usually distinguishes the structural crossing from the finished eye, and reading carefully repays the effort.

There is a simple physical way to internalise handedness. Lay a length of cord on a table and make a loop with the working end resting on top of the standing part. Now, without disturbing anything, slide the crossing along: notice that the identity of the loop is entirely determined by which strand is uppermost at that one point. Flip the loop over and the handedness appears to change, which is why instructions almost always specify the orientation relative to the standing part rather than relative to you. This is also why the reliable way to check a knot is to trace the working end with a finger from where it enters to where it leaves, rather than to compare the whole shape against a remembered picture.

Loops matter enormously in the mechanics of holding. Each crossing creates a point where one part of the rope presses against another, and it is that pressure — multiplied by friction and by the curvature of the rope around itself — that converts tension into grip. A knot with no crossings does not exist. A knot with the crossings in the wrong order or the wrong handedness will still look approximately right and may hold nothing at all.

sections.heading: Turns, Round Turns, Riding Turns and the Capstan Effect
sections.body:
When rope goes around an object rather than around itself, a different set of terms applies, and these describe how much of the object the rope embraces.

A turn is a single pass of the rope around a post, rail, ring or spar — roughly 360 degrees of contact. A round turn is two full passes, giving about 720 degrees. A half hitch is a turn around an object in which the working end passes under the standing part, so that the standing part traps it; a half hitch alone will not hold, but two of them in sequence, in the same direction, make the familiar two half hitches that secure a line to a post.

The term riding turn describes a turn that lies on top of another turn rather than beside it. Deliberately, this is the basis of knots such as the constrictor, where a riding turn traps the strands beneath it and produces a bind so tight the knot often has to be cut off. Accidentally, a riding turn on a winch drum or capstan is a jam that can take a long time and considerable care to clear, and on a powered winch it is genuinely dangerous.

The physics behind all of this is the capstan equation, sometimes called the belt-friction or Eytelwein equation, and it is the single most useful piece of theory in knotting. It states that the ratio of the tension on the loaded side to the tension you must apply on the other side grows exponentially with the total angle of wrap: T_load = T_hold × e^(μθ), where μ is the coefficient of friction between rope and surface and θ is the wrap angle in radians. The exponential is what makes it startling. With a modest coefficient of friction of 0.3, one full turn around a bollard, which is 2π radians or about 6.28, gives a multiplication factor of e^(0.3 × 6.28), roughly 6.6. Three turns give e^(0.3 × 18.85), which is around 285. A person holding with 20 kilograms of hand force can therefore restrain something on the order of 5,700 kilograms with three turns around a suitably rough post.

Two practical conclusions follow directly. First, adding wraps is dramatically more effective than pulling harder, which is why a sailor takes turns around a winch before hauling and why a rescuer takes turns around a bollard to lower a load with control. Second, friction is what a knot is made of. Every crossing, every turn, every place the rope presses on itself is a small capstan, and the reason a knot holds at all is the accumulation of these exponentially compounding friction terms.

The equation also explains why the same knot behaves differently in different materials. Modern high-modulus fibres such as Dyneema and Spectra have very low friction coefficients — slippery to the touch, and measurably so — which reduces μ and therefore collapses the exponential. Knots that are entirely secure in nylon or polyester can slip in these materials, which is why manufacturers of such lines usually specify splices or specific high-wrap knots rather than the standard repertoire.

sections.heading: The Nip: Where a Knot Actually Grips
sections.body:
If a knot has one working part, it is the nip. The nip is the place, or places, where the rope pinches against itself hard enough to stop the working end from sliding. Everything else in the structure — the turns, the tucks, the elegant symmetry — exists to create and maintain that pinch.

The mechanism is straightforward. When the standing part is tensioned, the curved sections of rope inside the knot try to straighten. Because they are wrapped around other sections, they cannot, and instead press inward on whatever lies inside the curve. That inward pressure is a normal force, and normal force multiplied by the coefficient of friction gives the maximum force that can be resisted before sliding begins. The greater the tension on the standing part, the greater the normal force at the nip, and therefore the greater the grip. This is the elegant, slightly counter-intuitive property of a well-designed knot: pulling harder makes it hold harder, up to the point where the rope itself fails.

Knots differ in where the nip sits and how many nips they have. In a bowline, the nip is the collar of rope that wraps around the standing part where the loop enters, and the small fixed bight — traditionally described as the rabbit's hole — that traps the working end. In a clove hitch, the nip is where the second turn lies over and pinches the first against the post. In a figure-eight follow-through, there are multiple nips distributed through the knot, which is one reason it holds so securely and also one reason it becomes hard to untie after heavy loading.

The nip explains several practical rules that otherwise look arbitrary. It explains why a knot must be dressed and set: an undressed knot has its strands lying in the wrong places, so the pressure that should fall on the working end falls somewhere useless, and the knot slips before it grips. It explains why some knots hold in stiff rope and slip in supple rope of the same diameter — stiff rope resists conforming at the nip and reduces contact area. It explains why a knot in wet or icy rope can behave differently, since water and ice change the friction coefficient. And it explains why knots in slippery synthetics need extra turns: more turns means more nips and more accumulated capstan effect, compensating for the lower friction per contact.

It also explains the failure mode called spilling. If the geometry of a knot is disturbed so that the nip opens — by loading in an unintended direction, by the rope being pushed rather than pulled, by a carabiner or rock levering a strand sideways — the pinch releases and the knot can run out under load in a fraction of a second. Knots do not usually fail by breaking. They fail by having their nip disorganised, which is a structural failure of geometry rather than a material failure of fibre.

sections.heading: How Much Strength a Knot Costs
sections.body:
Every knot weakens the rope it is tied in, and the amount is large enough that ignoring it is a serious error in any load-bearing application. Published figures for knot efficiency — the breaking strength of the roped-and-knotted system expressed as a percentage of the breaking strength of the plain rope — generally fall between about 50 and 80 percent. A figure-eight loop is commonly quoted at 75 to 80 percent, a bowline at 70 to 75 percent, a double fisherman's bend at 65 to 70 percent, a clove hitch at around 60 to 65 percent, and a simple overhand knot at 45 to 55 percent. These numbers vary considerably between studies, between rope types and between testing protocols, and they should be treated as bands rather than constants.

The mechanism of the loss is bending, not crushing. When rope curves sharply, the fibres on the outside of the curve are stretched further than those on the inside. Because load is shared between fibres only if they are strained equally, the outer fibres reach their breaking strain first and part, transferring their share to the next fibres in line, which then fail in turn. A knot is therefore a strength-limiting device by geometry: the tighter the smallest radius inside it, the greater the strain concentration and the lower the efficiency. This is the same effect that makes a rope running over a sharp edge so dangerous, and the same reason that pulley and carabiner diameters are specified in relation to rope diameter.

Two consequences follow. First, knots with gentler internal curves are stronger. The figure-eight beats the overhand largely because the extra turn spreads the bend over a longer arc, giving a larger effective radius. Second, the loss is roughly consistent for a given knot in a given rope, which means it can be designed around: engineers and riggers apply the efficiency figure as a factor when calculating a system's safe working load, alongside safety factors that in life-safety rigging are commonly 10:1 and in industrial rigging often 5:1.

Some honest caveats belong here. Published efficiency tables are usually derived from slow-pull tests to destruction on new rope in laboratory conditions. Real ropes are used, dirty, abraded and older; real loads include dynamic shock; real knots are imperfectly dressed. A knot's fatigue behaviour under repeated cyclic loading is much less well characterised than its single-pull strength, and it is an area where the honest answer is that the data are thinner than practitioners assume. There is also genuine disagreement in the published literature about the relative ranking of closely matched knots, because small differences in test method shift results by several percent.

The practical rule that survives all of this uncertainty is simple: assume a knot costs you a third of your rope's strength, design with a generous safety factor rather than a calculated margin, and never let a rope run over an edge sharper than the knot you were worried about.

sections.heading: Dressing and Setting: Turning a Shape Into a Knot
sections.body:
A knot is not finished when its strands are in the right topological order. It is finished when those strands have been arranged into their intended geometry and then compacted. These two stages have names — dressing and setting — and skipping them is the single most common cause of knots that perform worse than their reputation.

Dressing means arranging the parts so that they lie in the configuration the knot is designed to have: strands parallel where they should be parallel, crossings in the correct order, no unintended twists, the working end emerging where the design intends. A figure-eight follow-through, for example, is dressed when the two strands run neatly alongside each other all the way through the knot, never crossing over one another. It is undressed, or "sloppy", when they cross. Both versions are topologically the same knot and look broadly similar, but the undressed version has been measured in various tests to lose several percentage points of strength and is more prone to shifting under load.

Setting, sometimes called snugging, means loading the knot deliberately to compact it before it takes its working load. For most knots this means pulling each strand in turn, firmly, in the direction it will be pulled in use. Setting removes slack from inside the knot, brings the nips into contact, and establishes the friction that will hold. An unset knot has to compact itself during the first loading, and that self-tightening involves the strands moving relative to one another — which produces heat, wears the sheath, and can allow the working end to be drawn into the knot, shortening the tail.

The tail length question belongs here. A properly set knot with an adequate tail is stable; the same knot with a two-centimetre tail can invert or capsize under cyclic load and pull through. Life-safety practice generally requires a tail of at least ten rope diameters and often specifies a visual standard — a hand's width is a common field heuristic — precisely because it can be checked at a glance by a second person.

The habit worth building is a fixed inspection routine performed on every knot before it is loaded. Trace the rope with a finger from where it enters the knot to where it leaves, confirming that it follows the path you intended. Check that the working end exits on the correct side, since several knot pairs differ only in that detail and one of each pair is markedly weaker. Confirm the tail length. Confirm there are no crossed strands where parallel ones are intended. In any activity where a knot holds a person, this check should be done twice — once by the person who tied it and once by somebody else — and the second check is not an insult, it is the standard.

Two further points. Some knots are designed to be difficult to untie after heavy loading and some are designed to be easy; a bowline releases readily after load, a figure-eight can require considerable effort, and a knot that has been shock-loaded may be effectively welded. And a knot that has been fully set and then unloaded is not the same as a fresh knot: it holds a memory of its shape, and reusing it without re-dressing is a common source of error.

sections.heading: The Four Families: Stopper, Bend, Hitch and Loop
sections.body:
Named knots number in the thousands, but almost everything in practical use belongs to one of four functional families, and knowing which family a knot belongs to tells you what it is for and how it must be loaded.

A stopper knot is tied in the end of a line to prevent it from passing through a hole, a block, a fairlead or a belay device. It works purely by bulk. The overhand knot is the simplest and the weakest; the figure-eight knot is the standard because it is bulkier, easier to untie and less damaging to the rope; the stopper knots of traditional seamanship, such as the double overhand and the ashley stopper, exist because they resist pulling through larger apertures. The key structural point is that a stopper is loaded along the standing part in one direction only, and it neither joins anything nor attaches to anything.

A bend joins two ropes end to end. The sheet bend, the double sheet bend, the double fisherman's and the flat overhand bend all belong here. Bends are structurally interesting because both ropes carry the load and the knot must grip each of them, which is why most bends are approximately symmetrical and why they behave badly when the two ropes differ greatly in diameter or stiffness. The double sheet bend exists specifically to handle unequal diameters, adding a second turn around the thicker rope's bight to compensate for the mismatch. The reef knot, contrary to universal folk belief, is not a bend and must never be used to join two ropes under load: it capsizes readily and has killed people who used it as one. Its legitimate use is as a binding knot around an object.

A hitch attaches a rope to an object — a post, a ring, a rail, a carabiner, another rope used as an anchor. Hitches include the clove hitch, the round turn and two half hitches, the timber hitch, the prusik and the Munter. The defining property is that most hitches depend on the object for their structure: remove the post and the knot falls apart. This has a practical consequence that matters. Many hitches are direction-sensitive, holding well when loaded along the axis they were designed for and slipping when loaded sideways. A clove hitch on a smooth post under a load that rotates around the post will roll along it.

A loop knot forms a fixed eye in the rope. The bowline, the figure-eight follow-through, the alpine butterfly and the double bowline live here. Loop knots are what a person or a load attaches to, and they subdivide by where they can be tied: some require the end, some can be formed in the bight, and some, such as the alpine butterfly, are specifically designed to be loaded in three directions without deforming.

Two smaller families deserve mention. Binding knots, such as the constrictor and the surgeon's knot, hold something compressed rather than joining or attaching. And friction hitches, such as the prusik, klemheist and autoblock, grip a rope when loaded and release when unweighted — a category that behaves very differently from the rest and depends critically on the diameter ratio between the cord and the host rope.

sections.heading: Tying With the End Versus Tying in the Bight
sections.body:
One of the most useful classifications of knots is not by shape but by access: does tying it require a free end, or can it be formed in the middle of a line whose ends are both unavailable?

The distinction is entirely practical. Every knot that requires an end also requires that the end be free enough to be threaded, which means the rope must be unattached at that end, or short enough to pass, or the attachment must be undone first. In real use this condition frequently fails. A rope is anchored at the top of a pitch and disappears over a lip; a line is already made off at a cleat under load; a rescue rope is threaded through anchors at both ends. A knot that can be tied in the bight solves all these situations, and knowing three or four such knots is worth more in the field than knowing twenty end-tied ones.

The classic examples are worth naming. The figure-eight on a bight is the standard mid-line loop in climbing and rescue: form a bight, tie a figure-eight in the doubled rope, and you have a strong fixed eye anywhere along the line. The alpine butterfly is the preferred mid-line loop where the eye may be loaded in either direction along the rope as well as outward, because unlike the figure-eight on a bight it does not deform or jam when loaded from the side; it is the standard knot for isolating a damaged section of rope or for attaching a middle climber on a glacier rope. The bowline on a bight produces a doubled eye and can be formed mid-line. Most hitches — clove, Munter, prusik, girth — can also be made in the bight, which is why hitches are so common when working from an anchored line.

The inverse skill matters too: recognising when a knot genuinely needs the end. The classic case is the figure-eight follow-through, or rethreaded figure-eight, which climbers use to tie into a harness. It cannot be tied in the bight because the rope must physically pass through the harness's tie-in points, and a bight-formed loop cannot be threaded through a closed ring without an end. The technique is to tie a loose figure-eight in the standing part some distance from the end, pass the working end through the harness, then retrace the original knot backwards with the working end until two parallel strands run through the whole knot. That "follow the rope back through" method generalises: many end-required knots can be converted into a rethreaded version around a closed anchor.

There is a third category worth knowing about: slip forms. A knot tied with a bight in place of the working end at the final tuck becomes releasable by pulling the tail, which is convenient for temporary work and unacceptable for anything load-bearing, because the same pull can happen accidentally. The presence or absence of a bight at that final tuck is the entire difference between a permanent knot and a quick-release one, which is a good illustration of how much a single anatomical choice changes behaviour.

sections.heading: Rope Construction and How It Changes the Anatomy
sections.body:
The same knot behaves differently in different rope, and the reason lies in construction and material rather than in the knot itself.

Laid rope, also called twisted rope, is built by twisting fibres into yarns, yarns into strands, and typically three strands into the finished rope, each stage twisted in the opposite direction so the structure is self-locking. Traditional laid rope is right-hand laid, meaning the strands spiral clockwise away from you. Laid rope's structure has visible consequences for knotting: it hockles, forming kinks when twisted against the lay; it can be unlaid and spliced, which is the strongest possible termination at 90 to 95 percent efficiency; and some knots grip differently depending on whether the working end runs with or against the lay. Laid rope is also relatively stiff, which resists conforming at the nip.

Braided rope, in its simplest single-braid form, is woven from strands in a tubular pattern with no core. Kernmantle rope, the standard for climbing, caving and rescue, has a load-bearing core (the kern) of parallel or lightly twisted fibres, protected by a woven sheath (the mantle) that carries perhaps 15 to 30 percent of the load and takes the abrasion. This construction is supple, resists kinking, and conforms well inside knots, which generally improves knot performance and makes dressing easier. It also means a damaged sheath is not merely cosmetic — it exposes the core to abrasion, and a rope with core visible through the sheath is retired immediately.

Kernmantle rope divides further into dynamic and static. Dynamic rope, used for lead climbing, is designed to stretch — typically 30 to 40 percent at breaking load and around 6 to 8 percent under body weight — which absorbs the energy of a fall and limits the peak force on the climber and the anchors, generally to under 12 kilonewtons by standard. Static or low-stretch rope, used for rescue, caving and rope access, stretches perhaps 1 to 5 percent, which is what you want when hauling or ascending but which offers almost no shock absorption. Knots in dynamic rope tighten more and are harder to untie after loading; knots in static rope shift less but transmit shock far more brutally.

Material matters as much as construction. Nylon (polyamide) is strong, elastic, and loses roughly 10 to 15 percent of its strength when wet. Polyester is less elastic, holds strength when wet, and resists ultraviolet degradation better. Polypropylene floats and is cheap but is weak, degrades quickly in sunlight, and melts at a low temperature — around 165 °C — which makes it dangerous where friction heat is generated. High-modulus polyethylene fibres such as Dyneema and Spectra are extraordinarily strong for their weight, do not absorb water, and are notoriously slippery: many conventional knots slip in them, their melting point is low, around 145 to 150 °C, and their creep behaviour under sustained load is a genuine engineering concern. Aramids such as Kevlar and Technora are heat-resistant but suffer badly from bending fatigue, which makes them a poor choice for knotted applications specifically.

sections.heading: Three Knots Dissected by Their Parts
sections.body:
The clearest way to see how the vocabulary does real work is to describe familiar knots entirely in anatomical terms.

The bowline forms a fixed eye that will not slip or jam, and it is tied with the end. Its structure is a small fixed bight in the standing part — the collar or, in the childhood mnemonic, the rabbit hole — through which the working end passes, around behind the standing part, and back down through the same bight. The eye is the large loop below; the nip is where the collar pinches the working end against the standing part. Its virtues are that it unties readily after heavy loading and is fast to tie one-handed. Its weaknesses are anatomically visible: the tail lies on the inside of the eye where it can be dislodged, so it can capsize under ring loading or cyclic slack-and-load, and the standard remedy is either a stopper backup on the tail or a variant such as the double bowline or Yosemite finish.

The figure-eight follow-through is the standard climbing tie-in for exactly the anatomical reasons the bowline is not. It has multiple nips distributed through the knot, the two strands run parallel throughout so it is easy to inspect visually, and it is very difficult to load in a way that disorganises it. Its costs are also structural: the extra curvature makes it bulky, and after a hard fall the compaction at the nips can make it extremely hard to untie.

The clove hitch is two crossing turns around an object, each in the same direction, with the second lying so that it traps the first. It is fast, adjustable without being retied, and can be formed in the bight and dropped over a post. Its limits follow directly from having only one nip that depends on the object: it rolls along smooth cylinders, loosens under cyclic loading, and slips if the load direction rotates. It is excellent as an adjustable anchor tie in rescue and climbing, where the load direction is fixed, and unreliable as a permanent mooring.
steps: Take a rope and identify its parts before you start: the working end you will manipulate, the standing part that will take the load, and the standing end beyond it.

For a bowline, lay the standing part across your palm and make a small overhand loop in it — working end passing over the standing part, not under. This small crossing turn is the collar the knot will grip with; getting its handedness wrong produces a different, weaker knot.
Pass the working end up through that small loop from underneath, so it emerges on the far side.
Take the working end behind the standing part, above the small loop, so it wraps around the standing part.
Bring the working end back down through the small loop, alongside the strand already there, so both parts of the working end pass through the loop in the same direction.
Size the eye before tightening: the large loop that remains below is the working eye, and once set it is not adjustable.
Dress the knot: check the two strands through the small loop lie parallel and untwisted, and that the collar sits neatly around the standing part rather than skewed.
Set the knot by pulling the standing part and the eye apart firmly, then tug the tail to compact the collar.
Check the tail is at least ten rope diameters long — about a hand's width on 10 to 11 millimetre rope — and lies on the inside of the eye.
For anything holding weight, add a backup: tie a double overhand around the adjacent leg of the eye, or use a variant designed to secure the tail.
Trace the finished knot with a finger from where the standing part enters to where the tail exits, confirming the path matches the intended structure, and have a second person do the same.

sections.heading: How Knots Fail: Capsizing, Spilling, Rolling and Jamming
sections.body:
Knots rarely fail by the rope snapping inside them, though that is what people imagine. They fail by rearranging into a different shape, and each mode of rearrangement has a name that describes the geometry involved.

Capsizing is the transformation of one knot into another under load. The strands slip past one another into a new stable configuration that may hold much less well or not at all. The reef knot is the notorious example: pull sharply on one of its four ends and it capsizes into a lark's head that runs freely along the other rope. A bowline can capsize under ring loading, where the eye is pulled apart in two directions rather than loaded as a single strand. Capsizing is almost always a consequence of loading a knot in a direction its designer did not intend, and it can happen in a fraction of a second.

Spilling is the release of the nip, so that the knot simply opens and the rope runs through it. The usual causes are a knot that was never set, a knot loaded so lightly that the friction never established, a slippery fibre, or a strand levered sideways by a carabiner or an edge. Spilling is the failure mode most sensitive to rope material, and it is why knots that are perfectly reliable in nylon are unsafe in high-modulus fibres.

Rolling is a specific failure of hitches, in which the whole knot travels along the object it is tied to instead of gripping it. A clove hitch on a smooth polished rail under a shifting load will walk along the rail. The fix is either a rougher surface, more turns, or a hitch designed to resist it, such as a round turn and two half hitches, where the round turn takes most of the load through the capstan effect before the hitches even engage.

Cyclic loosening is the slow version of all of the above. Loading and unloading a knot repeatedly — a boat surging on a mooring, a person bouncing on a line, wind flogging a sheet — pumps the strands and gradually feeds the tail into or out of the knot. This is why tails matter and why knots on long-term loads should be backed up or replaced with splices or purpose-made terminations.

Jamming is the opposite problem and is a nuisance rather than a danger, except when it is not. A knot that has been heavily loaded, especially in wet or dirty rope or in a fibre with high friction, may become impossible to untie by hand. In a rescue or a retreat this can cost a rope. Knots vary enormously in this respect: bowlines and alpine butterflies untie easily, overhand knots and figure-eights after a hard fall may need a marlinspike or a fid, and some binding knots such as the constrictor are effectively permanent and are expected to be cut off.

The common thread is that all five modes are failures of geometry. This is why inspection is visual and structural — trace the path, check the exits, confirm the dressing — rather than a matter of pulling on things and hoping.

sections.heading: Reading a Diagram and Naming an Unknown Knot
sections.body:
Knot diagrams are a small graphical language with well-established conventions, and knowing them turns an ambiguous picture into an unambiguous instruction.

The most important convention is the over-and-under break. Where two parts of the rope cross, the strand that passes underneath is drawn with a small gap, so the strand that passes over appears continuous. That gap is the entire topological content of the crossing, and misreading it produces the wrong knot. Arrows indicate the direction the working end travels; a solid arrowhead usually means "pass through here", an open one "pull in this direction to tighten". Many diagrams shade or hatch one strand to distinguish two ropes in a bend, or to distinguish the working end from the standing part in a complicated loop knot.

Diagrams are also conventionally drawn loose, with the strands separated for clarity, which is the source of a great deal of beginner confusion: the finished knot looks nothing like the picture because the picture is a schematic of a knot that has not yet been set. Experienced readers tie the loose version first, compare the strand paths with the drawing, and only then dress and set it.

Naming an unknown knot is the reverse skill, and it is genuinely useful when you find a knot already tied on a rope you are about to trust. The procedure is systematic. First establish the family: does it terminate a line (stopper), join two lines (bend), attach to an object (hitch), or form an eye (loop)? Second, count the crossings and the turns, which is often enough to distinguish close relatives — an overhand loop has three crossings where a figure-eight loop has four. Third, trace the working end from where it enters to where it exits and note which side it comes out on, since several pairs of knots differ only in that. Fourth, check for symmetry, since bends are usually symmetrical and hitches usually are not.

Two cautions belong here. First, a great many knots have multiple names, and the same name is sometimes applied to different knots in different trades — "sheepshank", "thief knot" and "granny" have all been used loosely. The Ashley number is the closest thing to an unambiguous identifier, and when precision matters it is worth citing. Second, some pairs of knots are visually near-identical and dramatically different in strength: the flat overhand bend, widely used to join abseil ropes, versus the flat figure-eight bend, which is known to roll under load and has caused fatal accidents. If you cannot confidently name a knot on a rope you are about to load, the correct response is to untie it and tie one you can name, not to assume it is probably fine.

sections.heading: Building the Skill: Practice Materials and Method
sections.body:
Knot skill is motor learning, and motor learning has well-understood requirements: many repetitions, distributed over time, in varied conditions, with feedback. Reading about knots produces recognition; tying them produces competence, and the gap between the two is larger than most people expect.

The practical method is to work one knot at a time to genuine fluency before adding another. Fluency means being able to tie it correctly without looking at instructions, in under about ten seconds, then to tie it with the rope in an unfamiliar orientation, then behind your back or with your eyes closed, then in gloves, then in the cold and dark. Each of those conditions strips away a different crutch. Tying with eyes closed in particular forces the switch from visual copying to proprioceptive pattern, which is what survives stress.

Practice should be distributed rather than massed. Twenty repetitions a day for a week produces far more durable retention than 140 repetitions in one session, a finding robust across the motor-learning literature. It also helps to interleave: once you know three knots, practise them in random order rather than in blocks, which feels harder and produces better retention and better discrimination between similar knots.

A useful learning sequence for general purposes is: figure-eight stopper, figure-eight on a bight, figure-eight follow-through, bowline, clove hitch, round turn and two half hitches, double fisherman's, alpine butterfly, prusik, and a taut-line or midshipman's hitch for adjustable tension. That set covers all four families, includes both end-tied and bight-tied members, and handles the overwhelming majority of everyday and outdoor tasks.

Finally, deliberately practise the diagnostic half of the skill. Tie a knot wrong on purpose — reverse a crossing, leave it undressed, shorten the tail — and look at the result until you can spot each defect at a glance. Have someone else tie knots and check them. This is exactly the skill that matters when you are checking a partner's tie-in, and it is almost never practised.
ingredients: Two lengths of 6 to 8 millimetre soft-laid or braided cord, about 1.5 metres each. Two are essential because bends and friction hitches need a second rope. Soft cord holds its shape and shows dressing errors clearly.

One length of stiffer 10 to 11 millimetre rope, about 2 metres, so you learn how the same knots feel in a diameter that resists you. Retired climbing rope, given away free by most climbing gyms and shops, is ideal for practice and must never be used for anything load-bearing.

A short length of 5 to 6 millimetre accessory cord, about 1.5 metres, tied into a closed loop with a double fisherman's, for practising friction hitches such as the prusik. The cord must be significantly thinner than the host rope — roughly 60 to 80 percent of its diameter — or the hitch will not grip.

Something cylindrical and fixed to practise hitches on: a chair leg, a rail, a broom handle wedged in place, or a carabiner clipped to a bag handle. Practising hitches on nothing teaches the wrong muscle memory, because most hitches are structurally dependent on the object.
A sharp knife or a hot-knife rope cutter, plus a lighter or a roll of whipping twine, for cutting and sealing ends. Synthetic rope ends fray immediately and unusably if not sealed or whipped.

A reference you trust and can consult offline. The Ashley Book of Knots is the standard historical reference; a laminated pocket card of six to ten knots relevant to your activity is more useful in the field.
Optional but valuable: a second person. Checking someone else's knots and having yours checked is the single highest-value practice for any load-bearing use, and it cannot be simulated alone.

sections.heading: Limits, Inspection, and What to Do When Something Is Wrong
sections.body:
Understanding knot anatomy has boundaries that are worth stating plainly, because the confidence it produces can outrun the competence it delivers.

The first limit is that anatomy tells you about geometry, not about materials. A perfectly dressed, correctly chosen knot in degraded rope will fail, and rope degrades invisibly. Ultraviolet exposure breaks down nylon and especially polypropylene from the outside in, so a rope that has hung in sunlight for a season may retain its appearance and have lost a substantial fraction of its strength. Acids destroy nylon; a rope stored in a garage near a car battery is suspect. Heat glazes and fuses synthetic fibres — a rope run rapidly over another rope can generate enough friction heat to melt it, and a shiny, hard, glassy patch on a sheath is a retirement criterion. Most manufacturers specify a maximum service life of around ten years from manufacture even for unused rope, and far less with use.

The second limit is that no knot compensates for an unsuitable anchor, a sharp edge, or a load the rope was never rated for. Rope systems fail at their weakest point, and it is very often not the knot.

The third limit is one of honest uncertainty. The relative ranking of similar knots by strength is less settled than knot books imply; different testing laboratories using different pull rates, rope batches and knot-dressing standards have produced results that disagree by more than the differences they claim to measure. Fatigue behaviour under repeated partial loading is poorly characterised. Where sources disagree, the sensible response is to use the knot your discipline's professional bodies recommend, dress and set it properly, back it up, and design the system so that no single knot's exact efficiency is decisive.

The inspection routine that follows from all of this is short and should be habitual. Before loading any knot: trace the strand path from entry to exit; confirm the working end exits on the intended side; confirm parallel strands are parallel and not crossed; confirm the tail is long enough; confirm the knot is set, not merely shaped. On the rope itself: run it through your hands over its whole length, feeling for soft spots, flat spots, lumps, stiffness and glazing, and looking for sheath damage, discolouration and fuzzing. Anything you cannot explain is a reason to retire the rope, and a rope is much cheaper than the alternative.

When something is wrong, the responses are unglamorous and correct. If a knot is not the one you intended, untie it and start again rather than adjusting it. If a knot has jammed and you cannot free it by working the strands loose with your fingers or a blunt spike, and the rope is still needed, cut it and lose the length. If a rope has taken a serious shock load, retire it, because the damage from a high-impact fall is internal and not visible. And if you find yourself reasoning that a knot is probably fine, treat that thought itself as the alarm — the entire point of learning anatomy is that you no longer have to guess.

guides.safetyNote: Nothing in this guide qualifies anyone to rig a life-support system. Knots used to hold human weight — climbing, caving, rescue, arboriculture, rope access — must be learned under instruction, tied in rope rated for the purpose, inspected by a second person, and backed up. Every knot reduces rope strength, commonly by 20 to 50 percent, and a poorly dressed knot or one loaded in a direction it was not designed for can fail at a fraction of that. Never use hardware-store rope, decorative cord, or any line of unknown history and age for anything carrying a person, and retire any rope that has taken a shock load, been cut, glazed, chemically contaminated, or is simply too old to trust.

guides.title: The Overhand Knot and Its Variations
guides.summary: A complete account of the overhand knot: how it grips, how to tie and dress it, and the large family of knots built from it — figure-eights, double overhands, water knots, fisherman's knots, overhand bends and loops — together with strength losses, failure modes and how to untie one that has jammed.

sections.heading: Why the Simplest Knot Deserves a Study
sections.body:
The overhand knot is the knot almost everyone already ties without instruction. It is the knot that appears spontaneously in a garden hose, in headphone cable left in a pocket, in the end of a thread pulled through cloth, and in the tangle at the bottom of a bag of extension leads. Because it is so ordinary, it is easy to assume there is nothing to learn about it. That assumption is wrong in an interesting way: the overhand is not merely a knot but the seed from which a very large fraction of all practically useful knots grows. Learn what it does and why, and you have most of the working theory you need for the rest.

Consider the lineage. Add one more tuck of the working end and you have the figure-eight, the standard stopper and the basis of the climber's tie-in. Take two overhand knots of opposite handedness and you have the reef knot; take two of the same handedness and you have the granny, which is notoriously unreliable, and the difference between a serviceable knot and a dangerous one turns out to be nothing more than which way you crossed the ends. Pass a second turn before tucking and you have the double overhand, which is the building block of the fisherman's knots that join climbing cord, of the strangle knot that binds a bundle, and of the barrel knots that anglers rely on. Tie one around its own standing part and you have a half hitch, the ancestor of the clove hitch and the taut-line hitch. Tie one with the rope doubled and you have the overhand loop; tie one through a ring in webbing and you have the water knot.

The overhand also matters historically and mathematically. The Inca quipu, the knotted-cord records used across the Andes until the Spanish conquest, encoded numerals partly through clusters of overhand turns, with the number of turns in a long knot representing digits from two to nine. In mathematics, an overhand knot with its ends joined becomes the trefoil, the simplest knot that cannot be untied without cutting: it has crossing number three, meaning no diagram of it can be drawn with fewer than three crossings, and it comes in left- and right-handed forms that Max Dehn proved in 1914 are genuinely distinct rather than merely differently drawn.

Clifford Ashley's 1944 encyclopaedia catalogued around 3,900 knots across some 7,000 illustrations, and a striking proportion of the useful ones are overhand derivatives. Studying the overhand carefully is therefore not a beginner's exercise to be got past. It is the efficient route into the subject, because the same three mechanisms — curvature, nip and friction — explain every knot that follows.

sections.heading: What a Knot Actually Does: Curvature, Nip and Friction
sections.body:
A knot holds because friction between rope surfaces converts a large tension in the loaded part into a much smaller tension at the free end, and it does so with a leverage that is exponential rather than proportional. The governing relationship is the capstan equation, sometimes called the Euler–Eytelwein formula after Leonhard Euler's eighteenth-century work on belt friction: the tension you must hold, T_hold, relates to the load, T_load, by T_load equals T_hold multiplied by e raised to the power of the coefficient of friction times the total wrap angle in radians. Because the wrap angle sits in an exponent, small increases in contact produce enormous increases in holding power. Wrapping a rope one and a half times around a bollard, with a friction coefficient of about 0.2, gives a factor of roughly e to the 1.88, or about six and a half. Three full turns gives a factor near 43. A knot is essentially a capstan that uses the rope as its own bollard.

The second mechanism is the nip. Every functional knot contains a point where one part of the rope is pressed hard against another and the load itself supplies the pressure. Pull harder and the nip clamps harder, so the knot's grip scales with the very force trying to defeat it. In an overhand knot the nip is the short crossing where the working end passes under the standing part just before it emerges. That single crossing is what stops the tail from sliding back through, and it is why an overhand knot in dry hemp will hold a person while the same knot in wet polypropylene may not.

The third mechanism, curvature, is the price. Rope is a bundle of fibres, and when a bundle is bent sharply the fibres on the outside of the curve must travel further than those on the inside. Since they are joined, they cannot; instead the outer fibres take a disproportionate share of the tension while the inner ones go slack. Add to that the transverse crushing where one rope part presses across another, and the result is a stress concentration. The rule of thumb used in rigging is that a bend radius of at least four times the rope diameter keeps losses modest, and that losses rise steeply below that. An overhand knot bends the rope around a radius comparable to the rope's own thickness, which is why it is one of the weakest knots in common use.

Understanding these three mechanisms explains almost every practical rule you will ever be given about knots. Bulkier knots with gentler curves are stronger. Knots with more wrap angle before the nip hold slipperier rope. Knots that are cinched down evenly — dressed and set — distribute the curvature across more fibre and lose less strength than the same knot left loose and lumpy.

sections.heading: Tying the Overhand and Reading Its Anatomy
sections.body:
Before tying anything it helps to fix four words, because every knot description depends on them. The working end is the short end you manipulate. The standing part is the rest of the rope, the part that carries the load. A bight is a doubled section of rope that does not cross itself, like a hairpin. A loop is a bight whose sides have crossed, so that a closed circle is formed. Almost every instruction reduces to putting the working end through a loop in a particular direction.

The overhand knot is a single loop with the working end passed through it. What matters more than getting the form is getting the habit of dressing and setting. Dressing means arranging the parts so that they lie fair and parallel, without twists or crossings that were not intended. Setting means tightening the knot deliberately, pulling on each part in turn rather than simply yanking on the load side, so the knot takes its final shape under your control rather than under an emergency load. An undressed knot can lose ten to twenty per cent more strength than a dressed one, and in some cases, notably the overhand bend used to join rappel ropes, dressing is the difference between a knot that holds and one that rolls.

Leave a tail. The standard minimum is ten times the rope diameter, so about 10 cm on a 10 mm climbing rope, and for anything life-critical a hand's width or more is normal practice. Tails matter because every knot migrates slightly as it is loaded and unloaded, and a tail is the reserve that absorbs that migration.
steps: Hold the rope with the standing part in your left hand and 20 to 30 cm of working end free in your right.
Bring the working end across the front of the standing part to form a loop, deciding consciously whether the working end crosses in front or behind, because that choice fixes the knot's handedness.
Pass the working end through the loop from behind, so it emerges on the side you started from.
Slide the crossing along until the knot sits where you want it, keeping the loop open so the parts can still move.
Dress it: pull the two legs of the loop apart slightly so the strands lie parallel rather than crossing over one another, and remove any twists in the tail.
Set it: pull the standing part and the working end steadily in opposite directions until the knot is firm, then tug the load side once more to seat the nip.
Check the tail length; if it is shorter than ten rope diameters, untie and start again with more end to spare.

sections.heading: Handedness: The Overhand Comes in Two Mirror Forms
sections.body:
When you make the initial loop you must choose whether the working end crosses in front of the standing part or behind it. The two choices produce knots that are mirror images, and while a lone overhand behaves the same either way, the moment you tie a second one on top the choice becomes decisive. This is the single most consequential detail in the whole overhand family, and it is the reason two people can follow identical instructions and get knots of very different reliability.

The classic demonstration is the reef knot against the granny knot. A reef knot, also called a square knot, is two overhand knots stacked with opposite handedness: right over left, then left over right. Tied that way, the two halves lie symmetrically, each part entering and leaving the knot parallel to its partner, and the knot lies flat. A granny knot is two overhands of the same handedness. Its parts leave the knot at an angle across each other, it sits cocked rather than flat, and under load it tends to slip or capsize into a form that runs. The granny is the reason the reef knot has an undeserved reputation for treachery: much of the time when a reef knot fails, it was actually a granny.

The same principle runs through the family. A double fisherman's bend is two double overhand knots tied so their turns spiral in matching directions and the knots seat against each other cleanly. Tie one of them the wrong way and the two halves will not marry; the knot will look lumpy, sit unevenly and be harder to set. In webbing, a water knot tied with a mismatched retrace will show the tape twisted rather than lying flat, which is both weaker and much harder to inspect.

There is a genuinely mathematical version of this asymmetry. Join the ends of an overhand knot and you get a trefoil, and the left-handed and right-handed trefoils cannot be deformed into one another no matter how you manipulate the rope. Max Dehn established this in 1914 using the knot group; the Jones polynomial, introduced by Vaughan Jones in 1984, gives a quicker modern proof, since it takes different values on the two forms. So the handedness you choose is not a matter of appearance. It is a topological property of the object you have made.

In practice, the way to internalise this is to always tie your knots the same way, so the correct form becomes what your hands do without supervision, and to learn what a correctly dressed knot looks like as a shape rather than as a sequence. Experienced riggers rarely check a knot by recalling the steps. They check it by recognising the picture, and a mirror-image error changes the picture immediately.

sections.heading: Strength Loss: Why Rope Breaks at the Knot
sections.body:
A rope with a knot in it almost always breaks at the knot, and it breaks well below its rated strength. This is not a defect in the rope or in the knot; it is a direct consequence of bending fibres around a tight radius while crushing them sideways. Knowing the rough size of the penalty is part of using rope competently, because the published breaking strength on a rope's label describes the rope in a straight pull, a condition it will almost never be in.

Published figures vary between test laboratories, rope constructions and whether the samples were dry or wet, so treat all of the following as ranges rather than constants. The plain overhand knot retains roughly 45 to 55 per cent of the rope's straight strength, making it among the weakest knots in general use. The figure-eight, which is the overhand with one extra tuck and therefore a gentler internal curve, retains around 75 to 80 per cent. A bowline sits near 70 to 75 per cent, a double fisherman's bend around 65 to 70 per cent, a water knot in tubular webbing around 60 to 70 per cent, and a clove hitch nearer 60 to 65. A splice, which introduces no sharp bend at all, can retain 90 per cent or more, which is precisely why splices are preferred wherever the rope will be permanently terminated.

The mechanism behind the ordering is consistent. Where the rope enters the knot on the loaded side it makes its sharpest turn, and that is where nearly every break initiates: examine a broken sample and the failure is at the entry to the first curve, not in the middle of the knot. Fibres on the outside of that curve carry more than their share of tension, so a nominal load of 10 kN spread evenly across a bundle might be concentrated so that some fibres see two or three times the average. They fail first, the load redistributes to their neighbours, and the failure runs across the cross-section in a cascade that from the outside looks instantaneous.

Two practical consequences follow. The first is that you should choose the knot with the gentlest curve you can accept, which usually means preferring the figure-eight to the overhand whenever bulk and untying are not a problem, and preferring a rounder knot in stiff or large-diameter rope. The second is that safety factors in rigging are set with knots already assumed. Recreational climbing systems are typically designed around a static breaking strength of 22 kN or more for a dynamic rope, against realistic fall forces held below about 12 kN by the rope's own stretch and by belay slippage, and that margin already anticipates that the tie-in knot has cost roughly a quarter of the rope. Removing that assumed margin by using a much weaker knot, or by damaging the rope, is how systems that look fine on paper fail in reality.

sections.heading: The Half Hitch: An Overhand Tied Around Something Else
sections.body:
If you tie an overhand knot around another object rather than around nothing, you have a half hitch. That single change of context turns a stopper into the most productive hitch-making element in the whole subject. Almost every common hitch is either a half hitch, a stack of them, or a half hitch with its parts rearranged, and understanding the half hitch means you can reconstruct the rest rather than memorising them.

On its own a half hitch is weak and untrustworthy, because there is only one crossing and only about one turn of wrap angle. It will hold a light, steady load in rough rope and will spill immediately in slippery rope or under a load that changes direction. Its usefulness is almost entirely as a component. Two half hitches tied in the same direction around a standing part give the knot called two half hitches, which is a serviceable general-purpose hitch for tying a line to a post or ring, and which is in fact a clove hitch tied around its own standing part. Two half hitches tied in opposite directions give a different and less secure result, which is a further reminder that handedness is doing real work.

The clove hitch itself is two half hitches made around an object rather than around the standing part, with the two crossings trapping each other. It is quick to tie, adjusts easily, and is genuinely useful for temporary work such as starting a lashing or securing a fender, but it slips under a load that pulls along the axis of the pole rather than across it, and it can roll loose if the load cycles. Anyone using a clove hitch in an application where release would matter should back it up, usually with a half hitch or an overhand around the standing part.

Adding an extra riding turn to a clove hitch produces the constrictor knot, which binds so hard it is often easier to cut than to untie. Rearranging the turns so that two of them sit on the loaded side of the standing part produces the taut-line or midshipman's hitch, a friction knot that can be slid to adjust tension and then grips where it is left, which is what holds a tent guy line at the right tension. Stacking several half hitches along a spar produces a marline hitching, used for whipping and for securing a sail cover.

The pedagogical point is that a rope-worker who genuinely understands the overhand and the half hitch does not need to memorise fifty hitches. They need to know what problem each arrangement solves — grip along an axis, grip across it, adjustability, quick release — and then build the arrangement that supplies it.

sections.heading: The Figure-Eight: One Extra Tuck Changes Everything
sections.body:
Take an overhand knot and, before passing the working end through the loop, give the end one extra half turn around the standing part. The result is the figure-eight knot, so called because its outline resembles the numeral. It is arguably the most important single knot in modern rope work, and its advantages over the overhand are worth understanding mechanically rather than accepting as folklore.

The first advantage is strength. The extra turn spreads the rope's change of direction over a larger arc and a bigger radius, so the peak curvature is lower and the load is shared across more fibre. Where the plain overhand retains roughly half the rope's strength, the figure-eight typically retains around three-quarters to four-fifths. That difference — perhaps 2.5 kN on a rope rated at 10 kN — is available for the cost of one extra motion of the wrist.

The second advantage is that it can be untied after loading. An overhand under heavy load welds itself into a small hard lump whose parts have nowhere to move; a figure-eight has a larger internal geometry, so the parts can be worked against each other and levered apart. A climber who has taken a serious fall onto an overhand tie-in may need pliers or a spike; on a figure-eight, bending the knot back on itself to break the set is usually enough.

The third advantage is inspectability. A correctly dressed figure-eight has an unmistakable symmetric shape, with the strands lying in parallel pairs and no strand crossing another where it should not. This makes it possible to check at a glance, from a distance, and it is why climbing partners check each other's tie-in by looking for the picture rather than by tracing the rope. A figure-eight tied incorrectly usually looks wrong immediately, whereas a mis-tied overhand looks much like a correct one.

The figure-eight family mirrors the overhand family throughout. A figure-eight on a bight makes a strong fixed loop, retaining about 75 to 80 per cent. A figure-eight retraced, or follow-through, is tied loosely in the rope and then re-threaded backwards through the knot after passing the end around an anchor or through a harness, giving the same loop where you cannot pass a closed bight — this is the standard climbing tie-in worldwide. A double figure-eight, sometimes called a bunny-ears, gives two independently adjustable loops for equalising two anchor points. A figure-eight bend joins two ropes, though it is bulkier and more prone to rolling than a double fisherman's and is less favoured for that reason.

The one place the plain overhand still beats the figure-eight is where compactness matters more than strength or untying — inside a fishing lure knot, inside a stopper meant to jam in a small hole, or as a temporary mark on a measuring line.

sections.heading: The Double Overhand and the Strangle Family
sections.body:
The other way to elaborate an overhand is not to add a tuck but to add a turn. Make the loop, pass the working end around a second time so there are two wraps, then tuck it through both. This is the double overhand knot, sometimes called a double overhand stopper or, when tied in the middle of a line, a barrel knot. Add a third wrap and you have a triple overhand. Each additional wrap adds roughly a further two pi radians of contact, which by the capstan relationship multiplies the holding friction rather than merely adding to it.

As a stopper the double overhand is bulkier and much more secure than the plain overhand, and unlike the figure-eight it tightens into a compact barrel that will not pull through a hole much smaller than itself. It is the standard stopper on the tail of a friction hitch and on the end of a rappel rope, though many practitioners prefer a figure-eight or a stopper tied with a long tail specifically because the double overhand can be very hard to release.

Tied around an object instead of around itself, the double overhand becomes the strangle knot. This is a binding knot: it is used to close the neck of a sack, to secure a whipping on the end of a rope, or to clamp a hose onto a barb. It grips because the two wraps cross over the tucked part, so the load on the standing part presses the tuck harder against the object. The strangle is often confused with the constrictor, which looks similar but is built from a clove hitch with an added riding turn; the constrictor grips harder still and is generally regarded as a knot you cut off rather than untie.

The most important use of the double overhand is not as a knot at all but as half of a bend. Two double overhands, each tied around the other rope's standing part and then drawn together, give the double fisherman's knot, also called the grapevine bend, which is the standard method for joining two ropes or making a closed loop of accessory cord for a Prusik. The seated knot is compact, symmetric, and very secure, retaining roughly two-thirds of the rope's strength. For very slippery high-modulus fibres such as Dyneema or Spectra, whose surface friction coefficient can be as low as 0.05 to 0.1 compared with about 0.15 to 0.25 for nylon, the triple fisherman's is used instead, because those extra wraps supply the friction the material does not.

There is one more member worth naming. The surgeon's knot is a reef knot whose first half is a double overhand rather than a single one. The extra friction stops the first throw from slipping while the second is being made — exactly the problem a surgeon faces tying a ligature in slippery tissue, and exactly the problem anyone faces lashing a springy bundle.

sections.heading: Joining Two Ropes with a Single Overhand: The Flat Overhand Bend
sections.body:
One of the most consequential and most argued-about knots in modern rope work is the simplest possible way to join two ropes: lay the two ends side by side, tie a single overhand knot in both together, and pull it tight. This is the flat overhand bend, also called the offset overhand bend, the one-sided overhand bend, and, in a piece of gallows humour that stuck, the European Death Knot. It is used almost universally by climbers to join two ropes for a rappel, and understanding both why it is used and why it earned that nickname is a good lesson in engineering trade-offs.

Its advantage is the shape it presents to the world. Because both tails emerge on the same side of the knot — that is what offset means — the knot has a smooth, flat profile on the loaded side. When the joined ropes are pulled down over a rock lip or an edge after a rappel, the knot rolls and slides over obstructions instead of catching on them. Every symmetrical bend, including the double fisherman's and the figure-eight bend, presents a lumpy profile that snags. A stuck rope on a multi-pitch descent is not merely inconvenient; it is a genuinely dangerous situation, and the flat overhand's resistance to jamming is a real safety benefit that has to be weighed against its weaknesses.

Its weakness is a failure mode called rolling or capsizing. Under load, the knot can invert and progressively roll along the rope, each roll consuming a few centimetres of tail. If the tails are short, enough rolls will run the knot off the end of the ropes entirely. Published test results vary considerably with rope diameter, rope pairing, how hard the knot was set, and the test method, but rolling has been observed beginning at loads in the region of roughly 2 to 7 kilonewtons, well within the range a real system can generate. Testing work by Tom Moyer and others in the 1990s and 2000s was influential in establishing both the reality of the failure and the mitigations.

The mitigations are specific and non-negotiable if you use this knot. Leave long tails, with 30 cm generally recommended and never less than about 20 cm. Set the knot extremely hard by pulling each of the four strands individually with full body weight, not by a casual tug, because a loosely set flat overhand rolls at a far lower load than a well set one. Avoid joining ropes of very different diameters, since a large mismatch encourages the smaller rope to migrate. Do not use the flat figure-eight version, which looks like an improvement but in fact rolls much more readily, a counterintuitive result confirmed in repeated testing. Many practitioners add a second flat overhand snugged against the first as a backup.

sections.heading: The Water Knot: Webbing's Special Case
sections.body:
Flat webbing behaves differently from round rope, and the knot that suits it is a specific overhand variant called the water knot, also known as the tape knot or ring bend. It is made by tying a loose overhand knot in one end of the webbing, then threading the other end back through that knot in the exact reverse path so the two tapes lie flat against each other throughout. The result is an overhand knot with two strands running side by side through every part of it.

Webbing needs its own knot because it is flat. A round rope resists twisting in a knot by its own torsional stiffness, but webbing can fold, roll on its edge, or twist through ninety degrees inside a knot without much resistance. When it does, the load concentrates on one edge of the tape instead of across its full width, and the strength drops sharply. This is why the water knot is always described in terms of retracing and lying flat: the single most important inspection criterion is that no part of the tape is twisted anywhere inside the knot. A correctly tied water knot looks like a flat, tidy overhand made from a doubled ribbon.

The water knot's serious weakness is creep. Under cyclic loading, and especially in the stiff, slick tubular nylon common in climbing slings, the tails migrate slowly out of the knot. This is not a sudden failure; it is a gradual one that can proceed over weeks of ordinary use in a sling that is loaded and unloaded repeatedly. Left long enough, a tail works entirely free and the knot fails completely. Fatal accidents attributed to water knots backing out of old, unattended slings are documented in climbing accident reports, and the standard mitigation is uncompromising: tails of at least 7.5 cm and preferably longer, a hard set, marking the tails so movement is visible, and physically inspecting the knot before every use rather than trusting a sling because it was correct last month.

A tied water knot in tubular nylon webbing typically retains something like 60 to 70 per cent of the webbing's rated strength, though as always test figures vary. Where a sling will be left in place for a long time, or where the consequences of failure are severe, sewn slings made with bar-tack stitching are preferred because they retain close to full strength and cannot creep. The water knot's place is where you need to make a sling from a length of tape on the spot, or to join tape for a temporary anchor.

A useful discipline for anyone using webbing is to treat a knotted sling as a consumable that is inspected every time and retired without sentiment, rather than as a piece of hardware.

sections.heading: The Fisherman's Knots: Overhands That Face Each Other
sections.body:
The fisherman's family solves the problem of joining two ropes securely and symmetrically, and it does so with a construction that is pure overhand. Lay the two ropes alongside each other pointing in opposite directions. With the end of the first rope, tie an overhand knot around the standing part of the second. With the end of the second, tie a matching overhand around the standing part of the first. Pull the two standing parts apart and the knots slide together and jam against one another, each preventing the other from moving. That is the single fisherman's knot, also called the English knot or true lover's knot.

The single version is used mainly for fine line and for tying together the ends of fishing leaders. For anything that matters structurally it is superseded by the double fisherman's, in which each half is a double overhand rather than a single one, giving two wraps of contact instead of one before the nip. The double fisherman's, or grapevine bend, is the standard for joining accessory cord, for making the closed loops used in Prusik and Klemheist friction hitches, and for joining ropes where the join will not need to be pulled over an edge. It retains around 65 to 70 per cent of the cord's strength and is extremely reliable when correctly dressed, which is easy to verify: a correct double fisherman's shows two parallel diagonal wraps on one face and four parallel strands running straight across the other.

The triple fisherman's adds a third wrap to each half and exists for a specific material reason. High-modulus polyethylene fibres sold as Dyneema and Spectra are exceptionally strong for their weight but have very low surface friction, with coefficients around 0.05 to 0.1 against roughly 0.15 to 0.25 for nylon.
